frameworks.name: On-Time On-Budget Guarantee Offer
frameworks.definition: A home service pricing and closing strategy that raises prices 20% while guaranteeing delivery on time and under budget, contingent on no scope changes, and refunds the margin if guarantees are missed.

frameworks.name: No-Change Contingency Protective Clause
frameworks.definition: A pricing guarantee protection mechanism that explicitly conditions the offer on scope immutability, allowing the seller to renegotiate if the buyer modifies requirements mid-project.

frameworks.name: Maintenance Plan Upsell with Review Incentive
frameworks.definition: A continuity upsell strategy that bundles annual maintenance coverage at a fixed cost, covers repairs up to 2x the plan cost, and waives the fee in exchange for a five-star review and operator spiff.

claims.text: Home service businesses face commoditization because high demand and abundant supply create competitive pressure toward price-cutting and a race to the bottom.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Home service buyers' primary concerns are on-time and on-budget delivery, making these the dominant decision criteria in purchase conversations.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Raising service prices by 20% while adding an on-time on-budget guarantee gives the seller complete negotiating leverage against lower-priced competitors who cannot match the guarantee.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: The guarantee becomes the differentiation anchor; competitors who undercut price lose credibility when they cannot guarantee outcomes, shifting the buyer's decision from price to certainty.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi runs 20% net margins on home service work and can refund that full margin to customers if on-time on-budget guarantees are missed, protecting the base revenue.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Explicitly conditioning the on-time on-budget guarantee on no scope changes allows the seller to renegotiate mid-project without breaking the guarantee, because the contingency clause permits re-discussion when terms shift.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: The contingency clause resets the guarantee promise; when the buyer changes requirements, the seller can re-quote and re-commit to new terms, preserving both the guarantee's validity and the seller's margin.
bounded_by: Does not apply if seller initiates scope changes
Does not protect against delivery failures unrelated to scope changes

claims.text: Maintenance plans in home service businesses double the durability of the installed product (e.g., turf) by addressing wear-and-tear damage before it accumulates.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
bounded_by: Does not apply to products with inherent durability limits unrelated to maintenance

claims.text: A maintenance plan structured at the lowest price point to ensure adoption, then covering repairs up to twice the annual cost, creates profitability because repair markups absorb the guarantee spread.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Low barrier-to-entry pricing (e.g., $200/year) maximizes plan adoption; the seller then recoups margin through repairs covered at higher blended rates (e.g., up to $500/year in repairs covered). The asymmetry between what the customer perceives as free repairs and actual margin captured is the profit lever.

anchors.value: up to $500 per year (2.5x plan cost)

claims.text: Waiving a maintenance plan fee ($500/year in the example) in exchange for a five-star customer review creates a conversion lever that captures proof while protecting the seller's revenue by moving the cost from cash to review asset.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: home service business with digital presence (reviews matter)
claims.mechanism: Five-star reviews are the currency of trust in home service discovery; waiving a low-margin maintenance fee in exchange captures an asset (proof) more valuable to the business than the waived revenue, shifting the customer to 100% adoption because the perceived trade (review for free service) is asymmetrically favorable to the buyer.
bounded_by: Assumes reviews are visible and high-volume (applicable to homeowner-facing businesses, not B2B)
Requires salesperson to present the review waiver as employee/family benefit, not as owner discount

claims.text: Having a non-owner salesperson present the maintenance plan and frame the review waiver as a team spiff (benefit to named laborers Javier and Jose) dramatically increases adoption relative to the owner pitching the same offer, because it creates prosocial trust without appearing self-serving.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: salesperson is project manager, not owner
review waiver framed as team benefit, not company discount
claims.mechanism: A non-owner credibly advocates for the team without apparent financial self-interest; naming the laborers and attributing the spiff to them creates identity-level motivation (the worker benefits, not the corporation), making the ask prosocially compliant.
bounded_by: Requires clear separation between project manager and ownership
Fails if salesperson is perceived as owner or appears to benefit directly from the conversion

examples.text: A homeowner shopping two competing quotes: one lower-priced without guarantees, one 20% higher with on-time on-budget guarantee. The seller using the guarantee says: 'Did they guarantee time and budget? No one will. Well then I can do it for a dollar as long as I don't have to guarantee time and budget. With me, when you pay this, you know it will be done by this time and under this number, period.' This reframes the price difference as certainty insurance, not premium cost.

A customer requests mid-project scope expansion (add another edge, cover that area). The project manager says: 'Absolutely can I do it, I can't stick with this anymore but I just want to make sure you're clear—you just changed the terms. Yeah? Yeah, okay, I want that.' This allows the manager to reset the guarantee scope, protecting the margin while appearing flexible.

A homeowner buys landscaping. A year later, edges are frayed and turf is degraded (expected wear). The salesperson says: 'For $200 a year, we'll cover up to $500 in repairs, keep it maintained. It'll double the turf duration. If you ever sell the house, you don't want to replace it. With this, it adds to your home value.' The customer agrees because the pain of future replacement is reframed as preventable via maintenance.

The salesperson (non-owner project manager) says: 'Right now ownership's running a special where if you leave us a five-star review, the maintenance plan is free. If you do, the guys get a little spiff—Javier and Jose did an awesome job, it means a lot to them and their families. You'll get $500 worth of service for free.' The customer readily agrees because the trade feels like they're rewarding the workers, not enriching the company.

practices.text: Raise prices by 20% before anchoring a guarantee (do not discount from base price to cover guarantee cost; capture the margin increase as buffer).
Use the non-owner salesperson (project manager) to pitch continuity offers because the recommendation carries prosocial weight without founder bias.
Frame maintenance plan adoption with home-value benefits (longevity, resale readiness) rather than pure repair-cost savings.
Structure maintenance plan pricing as 1x cost with 2x repair coverage to maximize adoption while maintaining margin through repair markup economics.
